question: You Always Want the Smartest Model
content: Naval argues that intelligence is an 'unalloyed good' — you always want more of it. When models make mistakes, you don't know it, and they're always cheaper than a real person.
description: Your CFO proposes using a cheaper, less intelligent AI model for 97% of coding tasks and only using the frontier model for the hardest 3%. Based on Naval's argument, what is the flaw in this cost-saving strategy?
options: The cheaper model costs more in compute than the frontier model
When the cheaper model makes a mistake, you won't know it, and intelligence is too valuable to compromise on
The cheaper model is actually more intelligent than the frontier model for coding tasks
The strategy would violate the AI model's terms of service
answer: When the cheaper model makes a mistake, you won't know it, and intelligence is too valuable to compromise on
explanation: Naval says: 'When these models make a mistake, you don't know it' — and intelligence is an unalloyed good. Given the leverage poured through decisions, you always want the most intelligent model.

question: The Dinner Table Debate
content: Naval recounts a dinner argument where someone claimed you could use DeepSeek for 97% of tasks and only fall back to OpenAI or Anthropic for the hardest ones. Naval disagrees fundamentally.
description: At a dinner, a startup founder argues that DeepSeek is good enough for nearly everything — just run the same problem multiple times if you need more intelligence. How does Naval counter this argument?
options: DeepSeek is not actually cheaper when you account for the cost of running it multiple times
You don't know when the model makes a mistake, and you always want the most correct answer given the leverage you're applying
DeepSeek has a context window limit that makes it unsuitable for complex tasks
Running the same problem multiple times creates inconsistent results that are hard to validate
answer: You don't know when the model makes a mistake, and you always want the most correct answer given the leverage you're applying
explanation: Naval rejects the cheap-model-for-most-tasks approach because you never know when a model errs. With the leverage of capital, code, and people behind every decision, you want the best judgment every time.

question: When You Can't Tell Which Answer Is Right
content: Naval describes a key problem: when two models give different answers and you don't know which is correct, you'll trust the one you believe is smarter, and eventually stop asking the less intelligent model entirely.
description: You ask both GPT-4o and a cheaper model the same complex question. They give different answers, and you lack the domain expertise to judge which is correct. What does Naval predict will happen in this scenario over time?
options: You will run both models and average their answers for better accuracy
You will trust the model you believe is more intelligent, and eventually stop consulting the other one
You will ask a third model to break the tie
You will randomly pick one answer since you can't tell which is correct
answer: You will trust the model you believe is more intelligent, and eventually stop consulting the other one
explanation: Naval says: 'If I know one model is a little smarter than the next, and they both give me answers, often I don't actually know which is the correct answer. So if I know one model is a little smarter, I'm going to go with that answer, and eventually I'm going to stop asking the model I think is less intelligent.'

question: Gemini at Scale — The Underrated Contender
content: Guillermo Rauch shares data from Vercel's AI Gateway showing that while frontier intelligence dominates, Gemini models are super smart 'at the right performance-cost combination' — especially for non-coding tasks.
description: You need to deploy AI for a high-volume customer support automation system. Cost matters but so does quality. Based on Guillermo's experience with AI Gateway data, what model strategy might work best?
options: Use only the most expensive frontier model because quality is all that matters
Use Gemini models for support and browser automation because they offer the best performance-cost ratio for non-coding tasks
Use only open-source Chinese models because they are free
Avoid all third-party models and fine-tune your own from scratch
answer: Use Gemini models for support and browser automation because they offer the best performance-cost ratio for non-coding tasks
explanation: Guillermo says: 'Gemini — people don't get really excited about Gemini, but they put out models that are super smart at the right performance-cost combination. For a lot of tasks other than coding, interestingly enough, they're the best models.'

question: The Two-Tier Model Strategy
content: Guillermo describes a practical split: use frontier models for pushing the coding frontier, and use cheaper models (including Chinese models and Gemini) for support tasks, browser automation, and industrial production.
description: You are designing an AI deployment strategy for your company. You need both cutting-edge code generation and cost-efficient automation for routine tasks. How does Guillermo Rauch suggest splitting the workload?
options: Use one model for everything to keep the architecture simple
Use frontier models for pushing the coding frontier and cheaper models like Gemini or Chinese models for support and automation
Use only open-source models to avoid vendor lock-in across all tasks
Always use the cheapest model and accept lower quality for all tasks
answer: Use frontier models for pushing the coding frontier and cheaper models like Gemini or Chinese models for support and automation
explanation: Guillermo says: 'Any time I'm working to push the frontier, you need the best possible coding model. That's basically two or three models. The Chinese are certainly not in it.' For other tasks, cheaper models work fine.

question: The Monopoly Problem
content: Naval acknowledges that his preference for the most intelligent model is 'not great news' because it concentrates power among the top two or three frontier labs, creating a monopoly or oligopoly situation in AI.
description: A policy maker is concerned about AI market concentration. You explain Naval's argument that everyone will gravitate toward the single most intelligent model. What market structure does this predict for AI?
options: A highly fragmented market with hundreds of competitive AI models
A monopoly or oligopoly where the top few frontier models dominate because users always prefer the smartest
A market where open-source models eventually beat proprietary ones through community contributions
A market where every company fine-tunes its own model and no single player dominates
answer: A monopoly or oligopoly where the top few frontier models dominate because users always prefer the smartest
explanation: Naval says: 'Which isn't great news, because it means you'll end up creating a monopoly or oligopoly situation in AI. But I always want the most intelligent programmer.'

question: The Intelligence Unicorn
content: Guillermo reveals that Chinese models are 'certainly not in it' when it comes to frontier coding — despite all the hype, the real frontier work is dominated by just two or three Western model providers.
description: A tech journalist claims 'Chinese AI models are now competing head-to-head with Western frontier models on coding tasks.' Based on what Naval and Guillermo agree on, is this claim accurate?
options: Yes, DeepSeek has surpassed GPT-4 on all major coding benchmarks
No — neither Naval nor Guillermo sees Chinese models being used for frontier coding work
Partially — Chinese models lead on coding but trail on creative writing
The comparison is meaningless because Chinese models don't publish benchmarks
answer: No — neither Naval nor Guillermo sees Chinese models being used for frontier coding work
explanation: Naval says he doesn't know anyone who uses Chinese models. Guillermo confirms: 'The Chinese are certainly not in it' when it comes to frontier coding. Chinese models find use in support and automation, not cutting-edge coding.

question: Cheaper Models Have Their Place
content: Despite Naval's preference for the smartest model, Guillermo provides real usage data showing that cheaper models are used extensively — just not for frontier coding work. The key is matching model capability to task complexity.
description: Your team is debating whether to standardize on one AI model for all use cases. Guillermo has real AI Gateway data showing usage patterns. What is the correct approach based on his observations?
options: Standardize on the cheapest model because it handles 90% of tasks adequately
Standardize on the most expensive frontier model to avoid mistakes
Match the model to the task — frontier models for cutting-edge coding, cheaper models for support and automation
Use whichever model the individual developer prefers with no company-wide strategy
answer: Match the model to the task — frontier models for cutting-edge coding, cheaper models for support and automation
explanation: Guillermo's AI Gateway data shows both tiers are used: frontier intelligence dominates but cheaper models (Gemini, Chinese models) serve well for support, browser automation, and industrial production tasks.
